title: DC Students Post a Fourth Straight Year of Gains on the 2026 State Assessments
author: Josh Boots
summary: Josh Boots of EmpowerK12 analyzes Washington, D.C.'s 2026 CAPE state assessment results, which showed a fourth consecutive year of gains in math and English across every student group. He argues for tracking the career-ready Level 3+ benchmark and the share of students at Level 1, not just the headline Level 4 rate, because the pandemic hit lower benchmarks hardest. The analysis finds that achievement gaps narrowed, that a school's poverty rate is now less predictive of proficiency than at any point in D.C. testing history, and that post-pandemic cohort gains in math outpace the pre-pandemic trend. It highlights a historic single-year drop in students scoring at Level 1 in math. Boots attributes the progress to aligned citywide strategy, equitable funding, tutoring, and evidence-based math instruction such as the Capital Math Collective, and urges officials to sustain those investments.
points: Six in ten D.C. students met the career-ready benchmark in ELA and 51 percent in math, both up from the prior year.
The correlation between a school's socioeconomic makeup and its proficiency rate is the lowest in D.C. state test history.
Economically disadvantaged students posted annual math gains at nearly twice the pre-pandemic pace.
D.C. saw 1,500 fewer students scoring at Level 1 in math, a historic 13 percent single-year decrease.
Capital Math Collective grantees outgained non-grantees in math proficiency by a statistically significant margin after one year.
quotes: DC students improved for the fourth consecutive year, with gains in both subjects and across every student group.

Achievement gaps narrowed and student poverty is less predictive of school performance in math and reading. In fact, the correlation between socioeconomic status of a school’s student body and its proficiency rate is the lowest in DC state test history.
The pandemic hit the 3+ benchmark hardest. Proficiency rates fell further at 3+ than at 4+, and achievement gaps widened more at 3+ than at 4+.
The grades that fell furthest in 2022 have recovered fastest. Third grade, which dropped 21 points after returning from school closures and virtual learning, regained 16 points.
Economically disadvantaged students, who lost the most ground during the pandemic, produced annual gains at nearly twice the pre-pandemic pace.
Maintain investment levels. The equitable funding formula and the investments in tutoring and teacher development created this momentum, and sustained funding will carry it forward.
Four years of post-pandemic gains have shown what DC’s public schools can do when citywide strategy, funding, and instruction pull in the same direction
